subQuestions.questionText:
The value of inputs that are owned by an entrepreneur and used in the production process is called â€¦ cost.
A explicit
B implicit
C total
D average
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (implicit) (2 marks)
Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using resources owned by the entrepreneur in the production process, i.e. the value of inputs the entrepreneur already owns and uses, for which no cash payment is made.

subQuestions.questionText:
When average revenue is greater than average cost, the firm makes an/a ...
A economic loss.
B normal profit.
C total loss.
D economic profit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (economic profit) (2 marks)
When AR > AC, the firm earns more revenue per unit than it costs to produce each unit, yielding a supernormal (economic) profit above the normal rate of return.

subQuestions.questionText:
A market that is dominated by two producers is known as a/an â€¦
A duopoly.
B monopoly.
C oligopoly.
D trigopoly.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A (duopoly) (2 marks)
A duopoly is a specific form of oligopoly in which only two producers or sellers dominate the market.

subQuestions.questionText:
When the market fails to supply the product combination that is needed by consumers, it is called â€¦ inefficiency.
A pareto
B productive
C allocative
D technical
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C (allocative) (2 marks)
Allocative inefficiency occurs when the market fails to supply the combination of goods and services that best matches consumer preferences, meaning resources are not directed to their most valued uses.

subQuestions.questionText:
An index that measures prices of imported goods as they enter the country is known as â€¦ price index.
A consumer
B basket
C market
D producer
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D (producer) (2 marks)
The Producer Price Index (PPI) measures the prices of imported goods at the point of entry into the country, reflecting changes at the production/wholesale level.

Cultural tourism encompasses visits motivated by religious events, traditions, rituals, music and other activities unique to a given culture or society.

subQuestions.questionText:

A pollution.
B conservation.
C preservation.
D renewable.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B (conservation) (2 marks)
Conservation is the responsible management of natural resources so that they remain available for both present and future generations.

subQuestions.questionText:

The Stockholm Convention (Stockholm Protocol) is an international agreement that aims to eliminate or restrict the production and use of persistent organic pollutants (chemical waste) that are harmful to human health and the environment.

subQuestions.questionText: Differentiate between a natural monopoly and an artificial monopoly.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks. Comparative approach (2 marks per comparison point, max 8 marks):

â€¢ Natural monopolies exist due to barriers to entry that are economic in nature, while artificial monopolies exist due to barriers to entry that are not economic in nature.
â€¢ High development costs are a common reason for natural monopolies, whereas patent rights and licences are common reasons for artificial monopolies.
â€¢ Eskom is a natural monopoly as it requires billions of rands to establish and maintain electricity generation and transmission infrastructure, while SABC is an artificial monopoly as it requires licences for new businesses to provide radio and TV broadcasting services.
â€¢ Natural monopoly arises when a single firm is able to produce a good or service at a lower cost than any other business; however, artificial monopoly arises when a single firm is able to gain control of the market through government actions.
â€¢ Natural monopoly arises from the inherent characteristics of the market itself, but an artificial monopoly is created by external forces.
â€¢ Transnet and PRASA are other examples of natural monopolies, while Post Office and SARS are other examples of artificial monopolies in South Africa.

OR (separate discussion, max 4 marks per type):

Natural monopoly (max 4 marks):
â€¢ Exist due to barriers to entry that are economic in nature.
â€¢ High development costs are a common reason.
â€¢ Eskom / Transnet / PRASA are examples.
â€¢ Arises when a single firm can produce at a lower cost than any other business.
â€¢ Arises from the inherent characteristics of the market itself.

Artificial monopoly (max 4 marks):
â€¢ Exist due to barriers to entry that are not economic in nature.
â€¢ Patent rights and licences are common reasons.
â€¢ SABC / Post Office / SARS are examples.
â€¢ Arises when a single firm gains control of the market through government action.
â€¢ Created by external forces.

NB: If the second method is used, marks are allocated according to sequential presentation. If there is no correlation between the two types, one type can be marked up to a maximum of 4 marks only.
subQuestions.topic: Market Structures â€“ Monopoly â€“ Natural vs Artificial

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the effect of increased competition on the market.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point, max 4 points). Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts.

Positive effects of increased competition (2 marks each):
â€¢ As more businesses enter the market, more goods and services will be produced, which increases market supply.
â€¢ Increased competition forces businesses to focus on delivering quality products and services to stay competitive.
â€¢ Businesses may lower prices to attract more customers, which benefits consumers.
â€¢ Competition can drive businesses to be innovative and create new products and services to stay ahead of competitors.
â€¢ An increase in competition creates a more efficient and dynamic market, leading to benefits for both consumers and businesses.

Negative effects of increased competition (2 marks each):
â€¢ Businesses may lower their prices to remain competitive, which may lead to lower profit margins.
â€¢ Increased competition may lead to some businesses struggling to remain viable and being forced to close down.
â€¢ Business closures and reduced profit margins can lead to less supply of goods and services on the market.
â€¢ Increased competition can lead to price wars between companies and reduce their profits.

(Accept any other correct relevant response)
subQuestions.topic: Market Structures â€“ Effects of Competition

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the profit/loss that is made by the firm. Show ALL calculations. (From the graph: price/AR = R42, average cost/AC = R32, quantity = 100 units.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Method 1 â€“ TR minus TC:
Mark 1: TR = P x Q = R42 x 100 = R4 200
Mark 2: TC = AC x Q = R32 x 100 = R3 200
Marks 3-4: Profit = TR - TC = R4 200 - R3 200 = R1 000 (economic profit)

Method 2 â€“ (AR - AC) x Q:
Marks 1-2: (AR - AC) = R42 - R32 = R10
Mark 3: R10 x 100
Mark 4: = R1 000 (economic profit)

Note: Allocate 1 mark for the correct formula if the final calculation is incorrect.

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a well-labelled graph, explain normal profit for a perfectly competitive firm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Graph component (max 4 marks):
â€¢ Mark 1: Correct positioning and labelling of cost curves (MC and AC) and revenue curve (D=AR=MR)
â€¢ Mark 2: Correct indication of break-even point e (where MR=MC and AR=AC meet)
â€¢ Mark 3: Correct labelling of y-axis (Price/Cost/Revenue)
â€¢ Mark 4: Correct labelling of values on axes (e.g. P/R10 on y-axis; Q/100 on x-axis)

Explanation component (max 4 marks):
â€¢ Marks 5-6: The firm produces at point e where MR=MC and Q/100 units are produced at a price of P/R10.
â€¢ Marks 7-8: The firm makes normal profit/break-even because average revenue (P/R10) equals average cost (P/R10). TR (P x Q) - TC (AC x Q) = R1 000 - R1 000 = R0.

Note: Normal profit is the minimum earnings required to prevent the firm from leaving the industry. The graph must show D=AR=MR as a horizontal line tangent to the minimum of the AC curve at point e, with the MC curve passing through e from below.

subQuestions.memoText:

Any FOUR of the following (2 marks each):
â€¢ Continuously maintaining and upgrading existing infrastructure in order to improve accessibility of tourist destinations.
â€¢ Improving the accessibility and infrastructure in rural areas to allow these areas to realise their tourism potential.
â€¢ Using modern computer and communication technologies to efficiently market, promote and distribute travel and tourism products, services and information locally.
â€¢ Facilitating the funding of major tourism infrastructure projects that would have an impact on the development of the tourism industry.

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer BOTH parts in a structured essay:
â€¢ Discuss in detail the causes of market failure. (26 marks)
â€¢ Analyse the impact of minimum prices in the economy. (10 marks)

Essay structure: Introduction (max 2) + Main part (max 26) + Additional part (max 10) + Conclusion (max 2) = 40 marks total.
subQuestions.memoText:
INTRODUCTION (max 2 marks):
Market failure is when the forces of supply and demand fail to allocate resources efficiently / When markets fail to allocate goods and services efficiently.
(Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

---
MAIN PART â€“ CAUSES OF MARKET FAILURE (max 26 marks; max 8 marks for headings/sub-headings/examples)

EXTERNALITIES
â€¢ Externalities are costs and benefits to the third party that are not included in the market price.
â€¢ Goods that have negative externalities are over-produced because the cost to the third party is not included in the market price.
â€¢ Goods that have positive externalities are under-produced because the benefit to the third party is not included in the market price.
â€¢ Externalities are the costs and benefits (spill-over effects or third-party effects) that convert private cost and benefits into social cost and benefits.

Basic cost and benefit concepts:
â€¢ Private costs are the internal costs incurred by consumers and producers when they buy or produce goods and services.
â€¢ Private benefits are enjoyed by those who buy the goods and those who produce the goods (e.g., the family enjoys using the car and the producer earns profit).
â€¢ Social costs are the costs to individual producers and consumers as well as to society at large (e.g., pollution caused by waste products such as tyres, batteries, oil).
â€¢ No value is given for these extra or external costs because no market exists to price them.
â€¢ Social costs include both private costs and external costs.
â€¢ Social benefits are the total benefits enjoyed by producers, consumers and society at large.
â€¢ Social benefits include both private benefit and external benefit.

MISSING MARKETS
â€¢ Markets are often incomplete in the sense that they cannot meet the demand for certain goods.

Public goods:
â€¢ They are not provided by the price mechanism because producers cannot withhold the goods from non-payers and there is often no way of measuring how much a person consumes.
â€¢ Non-rivalry: consumption by one person does not reduce the consumption of another (e.g., a lighthouse).
â€¢ Non-excludability: consumption cannot be confined to those who have paid, so there are free riders (e.g., radio and TV licences in South Africa).
â€¢ Non-rejectability: individuals cannot abstain from consumption of public goods (e.g., street lights).

Merit goods:
â€¢ These are goods/services that are deemed necessary or beneficial to society (e.g., education, health care).
â€¢ Highly desirable for general welfare but not highly rated by the market, therefore provide inadequate output/supply.
â€¢ The market only takes private costs and benefits into account and not the social costs and benefits, leading to undersupply.

Demerit goods:
â€¢ These are goods/services regarded as bad or harmful for consumption (e.g., alcohol, cigarettes).
â€¢ Demerit goods lead to high social costs; therefore, the government charges sin tax/excise duties to discourage their consumption.
â€¢ The market tends to oversupply demerit goods.
â€¢ Some consumers may be unaware of the true cost of consuming them.

LACK OF INFORMATION
â€¢ Markets do not respond to changes in consumer demand if resources cannot be easily reallocated due to lack of information.
â€¢ Technical and allocative efficiency require that both producers and consumers have complete and accurate information about costs and benefits.
â€¢ When information is incomplete or inaccurate, it leads to wrong decisions about what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce, resulting in wasted resources.
â€¢ Producers might not know all the different technologies and production techniques available.
â€¢ Consumers might not know that a product is cheaper from other suppliers, or about the harmful effects of a product.

IMMOBILITY OF FACTORS OF PRODUCTION
â€¢ The supply of labour cannot be increased quickly because of the time it takes to be trained or educated.
â€¢ Labour takes time to move into new occupations and geographically, due to the long time needed to upgrade skills and family ties.
â€¢ Physical capital such as equipment, buildings, land and raw materials can only move from one place to another at a high cost.
â€¢ Technological applications change production methods (e.g., the use of robots rather than physical labour).
â€¢ With greater technological change there is an increasing need for workers to become flexible, update skills, change employment and work patterns.

IMPERFECT COMPETITION
â€¢ In market economies, competition is often weakened by market power because power often lies to a greater extent with producers than with consumers.
â€¢ Most businesses operate under conditions of imperfect competition that allows them to restrict output, raise prices and produce where price exceeds marginal cost.
â€¢ Monopolies and oligopolies restrict supply in order to maximise profits and can also prevent new businesses from entering the industry.
â€¢ Resources are under-allocated to the production of goods and services produced under conditions of imperfect competition.
â€¢ The government may choose to do nothing about imperfect competition and trust that large profits will attract competitors, or it can regulate the market through competition policy.

IMPERFECT DISTRIBUTION OF INCOME AND WEALTH
â€¢ The shortcoming of market systems is that it is neutral in the issue of income distribution.
â€¢ If the initial distribution of income is unequal, the final distribution will also be unequal, hence the market is failing.
â€¢ Unequal distribution of income is caused by varying skill levels and the ability to produce output.
â€¢ The market fails to ensure that everyone gets equal access to the output of the economy.
â€¢ Too many resources are used to produce output for the rich and too few for the poor.
(Accept any other correct relevant response)

---
ADDITIONAL PART â€“ IMPACT OF MINIMUM PRICES (max 10 marks; max 2 marks for mere listing)

Positive impacts:
â€¢ Minimum prices are set above the equilibrium price to benefit farmers as they will make adequate profits.
â€¢ Minimum prices allow agricultural producers to produce sufficient output to ensure food security in the country.
â€¢ More workers may be employed to produce more agricultural output, which will reduce unemployment in the economy.
â€¢ Increase in agricultural production may contribute to GDP which stimulates economic growth.
â€¢ More goods may be exported to generate more foreign exchange and reduce BOP problems.
â€¢ Businesses can be encouraged to invest more in industries covered by minimum prices, resulting in even more surpluses.

Negative impacts:
â€¢ Manufacturing businesses may be forced to procure agricultural raw materials at higher cost, which may contribute to inflation.
â€¢ Consumers may buy manufactured goods at higher prices, which may increase their cost of living.
â€¢ The standard of living for households may decrease as they fail to afford essential goods and services.
â€¢ The implementation of minimum prices creates product surpluses as quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, resulting in wasted resources.
â€¢ The surplus products are either dumped or sold at below-market prices in foreign countries in order to stabilise prices domestically.
â€¢ Sometimes surplus products are destroyed or used as animal fodder, as dumping goods is against WTO rules.
(Accept any other correct relevant response)

---
CONCLUSION (max 2 marks):
Taxes and subsidies can be effective tools for addressing market failures. However, the design of the tax or subsidy needs to be carefully considered to ensure that it is effective in addressing the market failure without creating unintended consequences.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)
subQuestions.topic: Market Failure; Price Controls â€“ Minimum Price

subQuestions.questionText:
Answer BOTH parts in a structured essay:
â€¢ Discuss in detail the consequences of inflation. (26 marks)
â€¢ How can the continued stages of load-shedding cause inflation? (10 marks)

Essay structure: Introduction (max 2) + Main part (max 26) + Additional part (max 10) + Conclusion (max 2) = 40 marks total.
subQuestions.memoText:
INTRODUCTION (max 2 marks):
Inflation is a considerable and sustainable increase in the general price level of goods and services over a period of time.
(Accept any other correct relevant introduction)

---
MAIN PART â€“ CONSEQUENCES OF INFLATION (max 26 marks; max 8 marks for headings/sub-headings/examples)

CREDITORS
â€¢ Creditors (lenders) suffer due to price increases because they get money back which has a lower purchasing power, especially if the interest rate has been below the inflation rate.
â€¢ Inflation harms creditors as they lose due to a fall in the real value of money.
â€¢ Changes in price levels affect debtors and creditors differently at different time periods.

DEBTORS
â€¢ Debtors (borrowers) receive money with a high buying power and pay back with money with a lower buying power.
â€¢ Borrowers benefit from price increases because they repay with money that has a low purchasing power.
â€¢ During periods of rising prices, debtors gain in real terms because the contract was signed in advance and cannot be changed.
â€¢ Debtors receive the money with a relatively high purchasing power and repay their loans with low purchasing power, unless interest rates are sufficient to prevent the situation.

SALARY AND WAGE EARNERS
â€¢ Price increases affect people negatively because their incomes are relatively fixed.
â€¢ Real wages fall sharply during periods of high inflation as a result of a decline in capital stock and a shift in relative prices.
â€¢ Inflation can impoverish large segments of the population by eroding real wages.
â€¢ Wages are the important component of wealth and the main source of income for many households, especially for the less well-off.
â€¢ The behaviour of real wages has a direct bearing on income distribution and the level of poverty.
â€¢ Retired people, pensioners and the poor will experience the erosion of spending power and eventually earn too little to survive.
â€¢ Wage increases are lower than the inflation rate increase.

INVESTORS AND SAVERS
â€¢ Assets with a fixed nominal value have a fixed return and lower purchasing power as prices increase.
â€¢ Purchasing power is reduced unless the interest rate is above the inflation rate.
â€¢ People who invest in negotiable instruments such as shares often benefit from inflation, because during periods of inflation interest rates are increased to encourage savings.
â€¢ Investors in assets with flexible market value gain when prices increase, because assets with a flexible market value increase at least proportionately to the rate of inflation.
â€¢ The prices of assets increase more rapidly than increases in the general price level.
â€¢ People save money for long periods to meet future expectations; these savings may be invested as fixed deposits, in the money market, as life policies or in pension funds.

TAX PAYERS
â€¢ With inflation taxpayers' nominal income rises although their real income remains unchanged, because taxes are levied on nominal income but not on real income, affecting purchasing power.
â€¢ When income tax brackets remain unchanged, inflation increases the average rate of personal income tax.
â€¢ Individuals will have to pay higher taxes even if they are actually no better off than before â€“ bracket creep leads to a redistribution of income from taxpayers to the government.

INDUSTRIAL PEACE
â€¢ Wage bargaining is accompanied by strikes and mass action.
â€¢ Mass actions can sometimes spill over into violence which affects society at large.
â€¢ Inflation leads to demands for increased wages as trade unions put increasing pressure on employers to raise wages and salaries.
â€¢ In extreme situations, in the presence of exceptionally high inflation together with a government determined not to yield to wage increase demands, widespread civil unrest would follow.

BALANCE OF PAYMENTS PROBLEMS
â€¢ Inflation has an adverse effect on a country's balance of payments.
â€¢ Inflation makes domestic prices increase, making domestic exports uncompetitive on international markets and South African exporters may lose major trading partners.
â€¢ The high prices of exports will discourage foreign businesses from buying South African goods, resulting in decreased exports and a loss of foreign exchange earnings.

UNEMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY
â€¢ The effects of inflation are uneven, because they do not benefit anyone and harm most â€“ some less than others.
â€¢ Inflation also tends to redistribute income from low-income groups to higher-income groups.
â€¢ Low-income groups do not have assets that can rise in value faster than the rate of inflation.
â€¢ Powerful groups such as trade unions, large companies and wealthy people are able to increase their share of national income at the expense of disadvantaged people such as pensioners, the unemployed and welfare recipients.

PSYCHOLOGICAL INFLUENCE
â€¢ Consumer and business expectations of what the economy holds in store influence their confidence within the economy.
â€¢ When their perception about the economy is negative, it will be reflected in poor consumer and business confidence and vice versa.
â€¢ High inflation rates decrease consumer confidence, resulting in consumers choosing to save their income rather than spending it.
â€¢ When consumers choose to save rather than spend, aggregate spending decreases in the economy, causing businesses to have limited expansion opportunities and thereby decreasing business confidence.
â€¢ When producers' costs increase due to spiralling inflation, it will decrease their competitiveness and the demand for their goods or services.

LOW INFLATION EXPECTATIONS
â€¢ Limit excessive wage demands by different labour unions because workers do not expect increases in cost of living in the future.
â€¢ Allow consumers to postpone consumption expenditure, thereby reducing pressure on price increases.
â€¢ Give households confidence that inflation rate will be low in future and encourage them to save more from income, thereby controlling excess demand.
â€¢ Reduce panic buying by consumers when they expect that prices will be stable in the future.
â€¢ Boost real interest rates which will encourage savings.
â€¢ Increase the burden on debtors which discourages them from borrowing money, due to the real interest rate.

HIGH INFLATION EXPECTATIONS
â€¢ Excessive wage demands by different labour unions because workers anticipate increases in cost of living will lead to producers increasing prices in order to recover extra costs of production.
â€¢ Prompts consumers to engage in panic buying when they expect prices to rise, thereby increasing pressure on prices.
â€¢ Make households save less, thereby leading to excess demand for goods and services.
â€¢ Decreases real interest rates which will discourage savings.
â€¢ Reduces the burden on creditors as they will receive their money at higher interest rates.
(Accept any other correct relevant response)

---
ADDITIONAL PART â€“ HOW LOAD-SHEDDING CAUSES INFLATION (max 10 marks; max 2 marks for mere listing)

Any FIVE of the following (2 marks each):
â€¢ Load shedding can lead to reduced production in many industries, causing shortages of goods and services which may result in demand-pull inflation.
â€¢ During load shedding, businesses may have to rely on backup power sources such as generators, which increase the cost of production resulting in cost-push inflation.
â€¢ Load shedding can lead to a weakened value of the rand due to a decrease in foreign investor confidence in the country's economy, hence decreasing aggregate supply and leading to inflation.
â€¢ A weakened rand value will result in an increase in key imported inputs which will increase prices of goods.
â€¢ Lower levels of investment contribute to stagflation through decreased employment and low economic growth, which can negatively affect the inflation rate.
â€¢ Load shedding can lead to supply chain disruptions, thereby causing inflation as businesses tend to pass on added costs to consumers.
â€¢ Inefficient allocation of resources due to load shedding hinders economic development and leads to cost inefficiencies which may contribute to higher prices.
â€¢ Load shedding may lead to increased government expenditure as the government is forced to invest in infrastructure such as power generators to address load-shedding issues, leading to inflationary pressures due to increased government borrowing.
(Accept any other correct relevant response)

---
CONCLUSION (max 2 marks):
Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money which means consumers can buy fewer goods, resulting in a decrease in the standard of living; thus it is important for wage increases to be higher than the inflation rate.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion)
subQuestions.topic: Inflation â€“ Consequences; Load-Shedding and Inflation
